title: Exact Euclidean SVP in BQP
formal: Do there exist a uniform quantum algorithm and a polynomial p such that, for every integer matrix \(B\in \mathbb{Z} ^{m\times d}\) with \(m\ge d\ge 1\) and linearly independent columns, the algorithm outputs \(z\in \mathbb{Z} ^{d}\setminus \{0\}\) satisfying ||\(Bz||_{2}=\min _{y\in \mathbb{Z} ^{d}\setminus \{0\}}||\)By||\(_{2}\) with probability at least \(2/3\), using at most \(p(\mathrm{L})\) elementary steps on every execution? L is the total binary encoding length of m, d and all entries of B.
why: A central test of quantum algorithms against worst-case lattice hardness.

progress.text: Randomized NP-hardness of Euclidean approximation within any fixed factor below \(\sqrt{2}\) provides hardness for exact search, without an unconditional quantum lower bound.
Published exact quantum algorithms improve exponential running times and state separate memory-access assumptions.
The revised Hessian preprint states improved expected exponential exact-SVP times, with exponential QRAM for its quantum bound.
A concurrent discrete-Gaussian sampling preprint also states an exponential exact-SVP consequence.
The critical response to the August DCP proposal is revised; the proposal’s stated lattice consequence concerns approximation rather than exact SVP.

definitions: The lattice generated by B is \(\Lambda (B)=\{Bz:z\in \mathbb{Z} ^{d}\}; d\) is its rank and m its ambient dimension. Its first minimum \(\lambda _{1}(\Lambda )\) is the minimum Euclidean length of a nonzero lattice vector. Full column rank makes this minimum positive and attained. The output is the signed binary coefficient vector z, so lattice membership and the corresponding integer vector Bz can be recovered without a real-number encoding. Any shortest vector is acceptable, with no uniqueness promise; the zero vector is excluded. Exactness means squared length equals \(\lambda _{1}^{2}\), rather than being within a multiplicative factor greater than one. Use the standard uniform quantum circuit model: a classical polynomial-time machine generates, from \(1^{\mathrm{L}}, a\) circuit on an L-bit input register, zero-initialized ancillary qubits and output qubits, using the fixed universal gates H, T and CNOT, followed by computational-basis measurement and polynomial-time classical decoding. H is the Hadamard gate, \(T=diag(1,\exp (i\pi /4))\), and CNOT maps |\(a,b\rangle\) to |\(a,a\oplus b\rangle\). Circuit size, qubit count, input processing and output writing are polynomial in L. No advice, oracle, pre-supplied quantum state or unit-cost access to an exponentially large memory is provided. Failure is allowed on at most one third of runs for each valid input; it is not an average over randomly chosen lattices. Malformed encodings and rank-deficient matrices can be rejected classically. Integer bases are the imported target; clearing rational denominators preserves shortest vectors up to a common scale and increases encoding length only polynomially.
answer_criterion: Prove existence of the algorithm with the stated worst-case polynomial cost and exact-search success on every valid basis, or prove that no such algorithm exists. Classical NP-hardness alone does not establish the negative answer for quantum computation. A polynomial-factor approximation, an algorithm for a promised special family, or an exponential-time speedup does not establish the positive answer.

context_blocks.title: The basis can hide a short vector
context_blocks.text: The vectors \((100,1)\) and \((101,1)\) are both long, but their difference is \((1,0)\). Since every nonzero integer vector has length at least one, this difference is shortest in their lattice. SVP searches all integer combinations of the supplied basis, rather than choosing its shortest column.

context_blocks.title: Exactness is a separate demand from probability
context_blocks.text: A successful run must output a genuinely shortest vector. Bounded error permits some runs to fail; it does not permit every run to return a slightly longer vector. Similarly, a quantum state encoding many candidate vectors is not the requested classical answer until a shortest coefficient vector can be extracted with the required probability.

context_blocks.title: Why classical hardness does not settle the quantum question
context_blocks.text: Micciancio proves randomized NP-hardness even for some constant-factor Euclidean approximations, hence also for exact search. A polynomial-time quantum exact solver would therefore put all NP decision problems in BQP, the class with bounded-error polynomial-time quantum algorithms. This is a complexity consequence of the reduction, not a proved impossibility: \(\mathrm{NP}\subseteq \mathrm{BQP}\) is not known to be false.

context_blocks.title: Faster exponential algorithms still leave the target open
context_blocks.text: The 2025 paper gives exact quantum algorithms with exponential dependence on rank and explicitly separates QRAM access. Hhan’s August 2026 preprint states expected classical time about \(2^{0.6039d}\) and quantum time about \(2^{0.5411d}\), up to lower-order exponential and polynomial factors; the quantum bound uses exponentially large QRAM. Kim’s concurrent sampling preprint also gives an exponential exact-SVP consequence. These recent claims were checked for scope, not independently proved. None gives polynomial time in L.

context_blocks.title: The recent coset claim has a different lattice consequence
context_blocks.text: Simon’s August 2026 DCP preprint claims polynomial-factor approximate SVP, which would not provide exact shortest vectors even if the algorithm were correct. Gupte, Ragavan and Zhandry’s response, revised on 1 September, claims a direct impossibility result for that proposed algorithm. The claim and response therefore do not supply a resolution of the exact-search problem on this card.

sentences: Can a quantum computer find an exactly shortest nonzero lattice vector in time polynomial in the encoded basis length?
The output must be a classical integer combination of the basis, with success probability at least two thirds on every valid input.
Randomized NP-hardness would make such an algorithm a major quantum complexity result, but is not a quantum impossibility proof.
August 2026 exact-SVP preprints claim faster exponential algorithms with additional memory details.
The disputed dihedral-coset proposal has an approximate-SVP consequence and does not settle this exact target.
